site.name: Camp Hale
overview: Camp Hale was a purpose-built high-altitude U.S. Army training center created during World War II in the Pando Valley. It became the principal Colorado training ground for soldiers learning mountain and winter warfare.

The site is most closely associated with the 10th Mountain Division. Soldiers trained in skiing, climbing, cold-weather survival, rough-terrain movement, weapons handling, and specialized equipment for mountain operations.

The wartime installation spread across a large developed valley floor with barracks, mess halls, warehouses, medical and recreation facilities, roads, rail support, ranges, stables, and other military infrastructure.

timeline.text: Army construction began in the Pando Valley and the Mountain Training Center moved to the new camp.
Mountain troops trained intensively at Camp Hale in skiing, climbing, cold-weather survival, rough-terrain movement, weapons deployment, and specialized mountain equipment.
The 10th Mountain Division fought in Italy after training in Colorado mountain conditions.
The Camp Hale area was later used for classified training of Tibetan resistance fighters.
Camp Hale became part of the Camp Hale–Continental Divide National Monument.

moreHistory: The high valley provided both room for a large military installation and immediate access to steep terrain, heavy snow, severe cold, and high elevations. Those conditions made the surrounding landscape part of the training system rather than merely a backdrop.

The camp included barracks, mess halls, warehouses, administrative buildings, theaters, chapels, hospital facilities, stables and corrals, motor-pool areas, rail facilities, ranges, ski areas, roads, and bridges.
Many original buildings are gone, but foundations, road patterns, rail traces, ranges, and the surrounding training terrain still help explain how the wartime installation functioned.
